Fix a length-$n$ finite promise computation from [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], with input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, zero-initialized auxiliary register $|0^{a(n)}\rangle$, circuit unitary $U_{C_n}$, and ordered output-wire tuple $O_n$. Let $P_{O_n}$ be the tensor-factor permutation that moves $O_n$, in its declared order, to the front, and let $W_n$ be the ordered tuple of all remaining wires ([[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]). Set
$$\psi_x:=U_{C_n}(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{a(n)}\rangle),\qquad v_x:=\operatorname{coord}(P_{O_n}\psi_x).$$
Here coordinates are in the ordered computational basis. In this definition, $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\rm root}:=\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\otimes}$ denotes the inner product on the reordered complete tensor register from [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]], linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For $z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}$ and $w\in\{0,1\}^{|W_n|}$, write $e_{z,w}$ for the corresponding product-basis vector and define
$$p_{C_n}(z\mid x):=\sum_{w\in\{0,1\}^{|W_n|}}\left|\langle P_{O_n}\psi_x,e_{z,w}\rangle_{\rm root}\right|^2.$$
The acceptance probability is
$$p_{C_n}(x):=\sum_{\substack{z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}\\A_n(x,z)=1}}p_{C_n}(z\mid x).$$
Equivalently, if $E_{A,x}$ is the diagonal projection onto the basis vectors $(z,w)$ with $A_n(x,z)=1$, then $p_{C_n}(x)=\operatorname{Tr}(E_{A,x}v_xv_x^\dagger)$; the matrix adjoint is conjugate transpose in an orthonormal basis ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]).

These are finite sums. The definition itself does not assert normalization, positivity of the resulting operator expression, or a probability bound; those consequences are the purpose of [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]]. No Dirac bra convention is used here: every amplitude uses the root pairing displayed above.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

A **promise problem** is a pair $(Y,N)$ of disjoint subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$. Its promise is $Y\cup N$. A deterministic solver must accept every word of $Y$ and reject every word of $N$, with either answer allowed elsewhere. The pair belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseP}$ if such a solver has a polynomial time bound on every input.

It belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseNP}$ if there are a polynomial $p$ and a deterministic polynomial-time predicate $V(x,w)$ such that every $x\in Y$ has some $w$ with $|w|\le p(|x|)$ and $V(x,w)=1$, whereas for every $x\in N$ every such $w$ has $V(x,w)=0$. The promise need not be decidable; either side or both sides may be empty. When $Y\cup N=\{0,1\}^*$, this is the ordinary language decision convention.

Write $\mathcal Q_n$ for the ordered tensor product of $n$ copies of the two-level register from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]], with $\mathcal Q_0=\mathbb C$. Fix a finite gate alphabet $G$. Each $g\in G$ has an arity $r(g)\ge1$ and a specified unitary $U_g:\mathcal Q_{r(g)}\to\mathcal Q_{r(g)}$. An operation model states which listed gates may be called and what access or cost is assigned to them; the matrix $U_g$ by itself is only the mathematical gate data.

For $n\ge0$, the circuit wire set is $[n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ in its displayed order and its state space is $\mathcal Q_n$. The computational basis word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})$ is assigned slot $\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$ from [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]], so wire $0$ is the most significant bit and the empty register has its single basis vector in slot $0$.

A gate occurrence on the $n$ wires is a pair $(g,(w_0,\ldots,w_{r(g)-1}))$ with distinct wire labels $w_j\in[n]$; the tuple order is the input and output factor order of the local gate. A layer is a finite ordered list of gate occurrences whose wire supports are pairwise disjoint. A unitary circuit is a finite chronological list $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ of such layers, with $L_1$ applied first and $L_d$ last; $d=0$ is the empty circuit. Its input, output, and terminally measured wires are specified as ordered lists without repetitions in $[n]$. This syntax specifies finite data only; the semantic action of gates on the full register is defined separately.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

derivations.claim: Let $\psi_x=U_C(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{a(n)}\rangle)$. Replacing the entire unconditional unitary $U_C$ by $\lambda U_C$ replaces $\psi_x$ by $\lambda\psi_x$. Since the root pairing is linear in its first argument, every coordinate $\langle P_O\psi_x,e_{z,w}\rangle_{\rm root}$ is multiplied by $\lambda$. Its squared modulus is unchanged because $|\lambda|^2=1$.

On a control-first pair of qubits, define $C(U)=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}$. For target $U=I_2$ and phase $\lambda=-1$, $C(U)=I_4$ while $C(\lambda U)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,-I_2)=Z\otimes I_2$. By [F2], this second matrix is implemented by applying $T$ four times to the control wire. On input $|00\rangle$, apply $H$ to the control, then respectively $C(I_2)$ or $C(-I_2)$, then $H$ to the control again. The first gate list maps $|00\rangle$ to $|00\rangle$ because $H^2=I_2$; the second maps it to $|10\rangle$ because direct matrix multiplication gives $HZH=X$ and $X|0\rangle=|1\rangle$. Each list uses only the fixed finite gates and the second is an explicit circuit realizing the target phase inside the control block.
The finite sums over $w$ and then over the accepting strings $z$ are therefore unchanged term by term. Thus both $p_C(z\mid x)$ and $p_C(x)$ are unchanged under an unconditional global phase.

Use these as the length-two circuits in two finite families, taking gate-free circuits with empty output tuples at other lengths. Let the promise pair be $Y=\{00\}$ and $N=\varnothing$, and let the total predicate accept exactly when $n=2$, $x=00$, and the measured control bit is $0$. Designate wire $0$ as the length-two output. The two families differ only by whether the target block is $I_2$ or $-I_2$. By [F1], the first has acceptance probability $1$ and the second has acceptance probability $0$, since their length-two outputs are the distinct basis vectors $|00\rangle$ and $|10\rangle$. Thus a phase applied only inside a controlled target block can change acceptance, even though the same scalar on an entire unitary leaves acceptance invariant.

A **full-list uniform quantum circuit family** is a sequence $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ together with one fixed deterministic one-tape Turing machine $G$ and constants $c\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N$ such that, on input the unary word $1^n$, $G$ halts within $c(n+1)^k$ transitions and its final tape is a valid self-delimiting binary description of the entire circuit $C_n$. The machine output convention is that of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]] and [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and running time is as in [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

The following fixed-order code makes the full circuit and its designated input/output wires effective. A unary natural $r\in\mathbb N$ is written $1^r0$, including the one-symbol code $0$ for $r=0$. A self-delimiting binary natural $r$ is written $1^{|\operatorname{bin}(r)|}0\operatorname{bin}(r)$, where $\operatorname{bin}(r)$ is its ordinary binary numeral with no leading zeros and $\operatorname{bin}(0)=0$. The header gives the input-wire count $n$ and total wire count $m$ in unary, followed by the gate count $g$ as a self-delimiting natural; validity requires $m\ge n$.

Each gate record consists of a two-bit label ($00,01,10,11$ for $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$ respectively), followed by one self-delimiting wire index for $H,T,T^\dagger$ and two ordered self-delimiting indices for CNOT. Every index is less than $m$; CNOT indices are distinct, with the first the control and the second the target. The list contains exactly $g$ records. After the gate list, an output-count self-delimiting natural is followed by that many ordered, pairwise distinct wire indices, each less than $m$. Parsing rejects every other label, malformed or out-of-range index, repeated output index, truncated field, or trailing bit. This defines a total decoder by returning a fixed malformed-code symbol on any invalid word; effective binary encodings and total decoders are as in [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]].

The gate labels and matrices are the fixed finite library $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$ of [[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]], with entries in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt2)$; CNOT is control-first. The remaining $m-n$ wires are auxiliary wires; their initial states are determined when a family is used in a computation model. This family convention adopts full-list generation. It makes no equivalence claim with indexed-gate uniformity and, in particular, does not assert that an indexed-gate generator can be expanded to the full list in polynomial time.

A **deterministic one-tape Turing machine with designated accept and reject
states** is a tuple
$$ M=(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\sqcup,q_0,q_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}},\delta) $$
such that:

- $Q$ is a finite set of states.
- $\Sigma$ is a finite input alphabet.
- $\Gamma$ is a finite tape alphabet with $\Sigma\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\sqcup\}$.
- $\sqcup\in\Gamma$ is the blank symbol.
- $q_0,q_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}}\in Q$ are pairwise distinct.
- $\delta$ is a function
  $$ \delta:(Q\setminus\{q_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}}\})\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{L,R\}. $$

Thus whenever the machine is in a nonhalting state $q$ and scans a symbol
$a\in\Gamma$, the value
$$ \delta(q,a)=(q',b,D) $$
specifies exactly one next state $q'$, exactly one symbol $b$ to write in the
currently scanned cell, and exactly one head move $D\in\{L,R\}$.

The intended tape is right-infinite and indexed by the natural numbers
([[def-computation-alphabet-and-word-convention]], [[def-function]]); the tape
contents, configurations, and one-step dynamics are fixed in the next items.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets, let
$$ e_X:X\to\{0,1\}^*,\qquad e_Y:Y\to\{0,1\}^* $$
be effective binary encodings in the sense of
[[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]], let
$$ M=(Q,\{0,1\},\Gamma,\sqcup,q_0,q_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}},\delta) $$
be a deterministic one-tape Turing machine, and let
$$ f:D\to Y $$
be a function with domain $D\subseteq X$.

The machine $M$ **computes the partial function $f$ under the fixed encodings
$e_X,e_Y$** if:

- for every $x\in D$, the computation of $M$ on input $e_X(x)$ halts and its
  final configuration outputs the binary word $e_Y(f(x))$, and
- for every $x\in X\setminus D$, the computation of $M$ on input $e_X(x)$
  diverges.

Thus the machine's input and output are ordinary finite binary words, while the
mathematical function lives on the underlying sets $X$ and $Y$ through the
chosen encodings.

derivations.claim: Initially the input $1^n$ occupies $n$ cells. In $T(n)$ transitions the head visits at most $T(n)+1$ additional positions, and each transition writes only one symbol by [F2]. At halting, the output convention [F3] therefore gives a binary word of length at most $n+T(n)+1$. The description is self-delimiting by [F1], so the number of its symbols is bounded by this polynomial quantity.

Each gate record contains at least one symbol, so its number of gates is no greater than the description length. The total wire count is explicitly unary in the same description, so it too is no greater than the description length. With $T(n)\le c(n+1)^k$, both quantities are $O(n+c(n+1)^k+1)$ and hence polynomial in $n$. The argument makes no claim that an indexed-gate generator can be converted to a full list.

Let $\Pi=(Y,N)$ be a promise problem: $Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$ are disjoint, and no answer is required outside $Y\cup N$ ([[def-promise-problem]]). For every input length $n\ge0$, let $a(n)\in\mathbb N$ be the number of auxiliary qubits. The $n$ input wires are ordered with the first wire most significant: for $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})$, $|x\rangle$ is the computational-basis vector indexed by
$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)=\sum_{k<n}x_k2^{n-1-k}$$
([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]], [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]). The auxiliary register has $a(n)$ wires and is initialized to $|0^{a(n)}\rangle$. When $n=0$ or $a(n)=0$, the corresponding zero-qubit register is the one-dimensional space $\mathbb C$, not the zero vector space.

For each $n$, a finite circuit $C_n$ acts on the ordered register of $n+a(n)$ wires and has the unitary denotation $U_{C_n}$ specified by [[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]] and [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]]. The circuit syntax designates an ordered tuple of distinct output-wire indices; an acceptance specification uses that same tuple $O_n$, whose indices lie in $\{0,\ldots,n+a(n)-1\}$. It consists of this tuple and a total predicate $A_n(x,z)\in\{0,1\}$ for $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ and $z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}$. The tuple may be empty; then its measured output set contains only the empty word. Auxiliary wires are initialized to zero, but this definition does not require them to return to zero after the computation; that stronger clean-ancilla condition is defined in [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]].

A **finite quantum promise computation** is the data $(\Pi,(C_n)_{n\ge0},a,O,A)$ with these registers and predicates. Its output is classical: measure only the named output wires in the computational basis and accept exactly when $A_n(x,z)=1$. No intermediate measurement is part of this base model. Unless a full-list uniformity condition is imposed separately, the family need not be generated uniformly. When uniformity or cost is claimed, $A$ is supplied by one fixed deterministic Turing machine with an explicit polynomial worst-case time bound in the encoded pair $(x,z)$ ([[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]]). This is a mathematical finite-circuit model and makes no assertion about physical realization.

Fix a length-$n$ finite promise computation from [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], with input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, zero-initialized auxiliary register $|0^{a(n)}\rangle$, circuit unitary $U_{C_n}$, and ordered output-wire tuple $O_n$. Let $P_{O_n}$ be the tensor-factor permutation that moves $O_n$, in its declared order, to the front, and let $W_n$ be the ordered tuple of all remaining wires ([[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]). Set
$$\psi_x:=U_{C_n}(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{a(n)}\rangle),\qquad v_x:=\operatorname{coord}(P_{O_n}\psi_x).$$
Here coordinates are in the ordered computational basis. In this definition, $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\rm root}:=\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\otimes}$ denotes the inner product on the reordered complete tensor register from [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]], linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For $z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}$ and $w\in\{0,1\}^{|W_n|}$, write $e_{z,w}$ for the corresponding product-basis vector and define
$$p_{C_n}(z\mid x):=\sum_{w\in\{0,1\}^{|W_n|}}\left|\langle P_{O_n}\psi_x,e_{z,w}\rangle_{\rm root}\right|^2.$$
The acceptance probability is
$$p_{C_n}(x):=\sum_{\substack{z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}\\A_n(x,z)=1}}p_{C_n}(z\mid x).$$
Equivalently, if $E_{A,x}$ is the diagonal projection onto the basis vectors $(z,w)$ with $A_n(x,z)=1$, then $p_{C_n}(x)=\operatorname{Tr}(E_{A,x}v_xv_x^\dagger)$; the matrix adjoint is conjugate transpose in an orthonormal basis ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]).

These are finite sums. The definition itself does not assert normalization, positivity of the resulting operator expression, or a probability bound; those consequences are the purpose of [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]]. No Dirac bra convention is used here: every amplitude uses the root pairing displayed above.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Write $\mathcal Q_n$ for the ordered tensor product of $n$ copies of the two-level register from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]], with $\mathcal Q_0=\mathbb C$. Fix a finite gate alphabet $G$. Each $g\in G$ has an arity $r(g)\ge1$ and a specified unitary $U_g:\mathcal Q_{r(g)}\to\mathcal Q_{r(g)}$. An operation model states which listed gates may be called and what access or cost is assigned to them; the matrix $U_g$ by itself is only the mathematical gate data.

For $n\ge0$, the circuit wire set is $[n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ in its displayed order and its state space is $\mathcal Q_n$. The computational basis word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})$ is assigned slot $\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$ from [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]], so wire $0$ is the most significant bit and the empty register has its single basis vector in slot $0$.

A gate occurrence on the $n$ wires is a pair $(g,(w_0,\ldots,w_{r(g)-1}))$ with distinct wire labels $w_j\in[n]$; the tuple order is the input and output factor order of the local gate. A layer is a finite ordered list of gate occurrences whose wire supports are pairwise disjoint. A unitary circuit is a finite chronological list $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ of such layers, with $L_1$ applied first and $L_d$ last; $d=0$ is the empty circuit. Its input, output, and terminally measured wires are specified as ordered lists without repetitions in $[n]$. This syntax specifies finite data only; the semantic action of gates on the full register is defined separately.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

derivations.claim: Write $\psi_x=U_{C_n}(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{a(n)}\rangle)$ and $\varphi=P_{O_n}\psi_x$. The input and zero-auxiliary vector has norm one by the computational-basis orthonormality in [F3]. By [A1] the circuit denotation is unitary, so it preserves norm. The permutation in [F4] bijects an orthonormal product basis; expanding in that basis and applying [F5] shows that it also preserves norm. Hence $\|\varphi\|^2=1$.

Expand $\varphi=\sum_{z,w}c_{z,w}e_{z,w}$ in the finite product basis, where $c_{z,w}=\langle\varphi,e_{z,w}\rangle_{\rm root}$ by [F5] and [F6]. Parseval gives $\sum_{z,w}|c_{z,w}|^2=1$. Each $p_{C_n}(z\mid x)=\sum_w|c_{z,w}|^2$ is nonnegative, and summing over $z$ gives one. By [F13] these weights form a finite probability space on the output strings. Its acceptance event is $\{z:A_n(x,z)=1\}$, so its probability is $p_{C_n}(x)$ and lies in $[0,1]$.

Let $\rho$ be the endomorphism with coordinate matrix $vv^\dagger$, where $v=(c_{z,w})_{z,w}$. This matrix is Hermitian, and for every coordinate vector $y$, $\langle\rho y,y\rangle_{\rm root}=y^\dagger vv^\dagger y=|v^\dagger y|^2\ge0$. Also $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=\sum_{z,w}|c_{z,w}|^2=1$ by [F11] and step 2.1. Thus $\rho$ is a density operator by [F7]. Put $\rho_O=\operatorname{Tr}_W\rho$. Its entries are $\sum_w c_{z,w}\overline{c_{z',w}}$ by [F9], so $(\rho_O)_{z,z'}=\overline{(\rho_O)_{z',z}}$. For any output-register vector $u$, the root pairing gives $\langle\rho_Ou,u\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_w|\sum_z\overline{c_{z,w}}u_z|^2\ge0$; its trace is $\sum_{z,w}|c_{z,w}|^2=1$. Therefore $\rho_O$ is a density operator, including when $O_n$ or $W_n$ is empty.

For each output string $z$, let $P_z$ be the coordinate projection that fixes the output basis vector $e_z$ and annihilates every $e_{z'}$ with $z'\ne z$. The product basis in [F3] and [F4] makes these nonnegative orthogonal projections with $\sum_zP_z=I$. They form the finite computational-basis POVM. By [F8], [F10], [F11], and [F12], its outcome weight is $$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_OP_z)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(P_z\otimes I_W))=\sum_w|c_{z,w}|^2=p_{C_n}(z\mid x),$$ where the middle equality is the diagonal trace in the product basis and [F2] gives the last equality. Summing over the accepting outputs identifies its event probability with $p_{C_n}(x)$. If $O_n$ is empty, its output set has the single empty string and $P_z=I_{\mathbb C}$; if $W_n$ is empty, the sum over $w$ has its single empty-string term. The same formulas cover both cases.

**Inputs.** In ordinary mode, a full-list uniform family generator $G$ in the exact fixed-library format of [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]; or, in oracle mode, an oracle-aware full-list generator and its granted access specification as in [[def-qc-oracle-full-list-circuit-family]]. In either mode supply a total deterministic acceptance-predicate machine $A$ and explicit polynomial clock bounds, with zero auxiliary initialization, output tuples, and acceptance as in [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]] and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]]; machines that output exact binary rationals $\alpha(n),\beta(n),\delta(n)$ with explicit polynomial clock bounds; and a fixed positive integer-valued polynomial $s(n)$ with an exact rational-coefficient representation. The machine descriptions and clock bounds are fixed parts of the input data, and each rational output has polynomial bit length. Valid inputs satisfy, for every $n$,
$$0\le \beta(n)<\alpha(n)\le1,\qquad \alpha(n)-\beta(n)\ge\frac1{s(n)},\qquad 0<\delta(n)\le\frac12.$$
The procedure checks the clock and syntax at each requested length and returns INVALID if a run exceeds its supplied clock, a code is malformed, or any displayed inequality fails. Its domain consists of descriptions whose stated polynomial bounds and inequalities hold for all $n$; the procedure does not decide that global validity property for arbitrary machine descriptions.

**Instructions at length $n$.**

1. Run the supplied machines within their polynomial clocks to obtain the full description of $C_n$, $\alpha=\alpha(n)$, $\beta=\beta(n)$, and $\delta=u/v$ with positive integers $u,v$. In oracle mode, also compare the printed port descriptors with the supplied access specification at length $n$; on any mismatch return INVALID. Evaluate $s(n)$ exactly from its fixed rational-coefficient polynomial. Check that it is a positive integer, check exact rational syntax, and check the validity inequalities by integer arithmetic; on failure return INVALID.
2. Let $\ell(v)$ be the number of binary digits of $v$ and set
$$r:=2s^2\bigl(\ell(v)+1\bigr).$$
This is a positive integer. No logarithm or irrational ceiling is evaluated.
3. Allocate $r$ disjoint copies of the entire $C_n$ wire register in block order, with block $1$ first. Put the classical-basis input $|x\rangle$ on the first block's first $n$ wires; initialize every other wire to zero. For $j=2,\ldots,r$ in increasing order, and then $i=0,\ldots,n-1$ in increasing order, append a CNOT from wire $i$ of block $1$ to wire $i$ of block $j$, with the first wire as control. These operations map $|x\rangle|0^n\rangle^{\otimes(r-1)}$ to $|x\rangle^{\otimes r}$ and do not clone arbitrary superpositions. Then, for blocks $j=1,\ldots,r$ in order, append the records of $C_n$ in their supplied chronological order, shifting each wire index by $(j-1)w(C_n)$. This serializes each base circuit's records; gates listed in a common layer have disjoint supports, so serialization preserves its denotation. Keep the first block's $n$ input wires first in the output wire order and encode input count $n$; every other wire is auxiliary. In oracle mode, retain each slot's port and granted variant, shift only its ordered wire indices by the block offset, and copy the access descriptors once. The added CNOTs are ordinary records, never query slots. The repeated circuit has $r w(C_n)$ wires and $r g(C_n)+n(r-1)$ operation occurrences; in oracle mode its ordinary count is $r g_{\rm ord}(C_n)+n(r-1)$.
4. Concatenate the $r$ copies of the declared output tuple in copy order and measure that tuple at the final readout. For measured strings $z_1,\ldots,z_r$, compute $S=\#\{i:A_n(x,z_i)=1\}$. The single total output predicate returns YES exactly when $2S\ge r(\alpha+\beta)$, evaluated exactly: if $\alpha=A/B$ and $\beta=C/D$ with positive denominators, compare $2SBD$ with $r(AD+CB)$. Return NO otherwise.

The output is one full-list repeated circuit in the input mode's format and its total classical predicate. Ordinary mode uses only the original fixed library. In oracle mode every base port/variant occurrence is repeated $r$ times: $N_{j,v}$, raw call counts $q_j$, and charged query costs $Q_j$ all scale by $r$, with unchanged grants and per-call charges ([[def-qc-oracle-full-list-circuit-family]]). Query costs remain separate from ordinary gates and classical bit costs ([[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]). The endpoint comparison is classical postprocessing, not an intermediate measurement or coherent amplitude-amplification step. Correctness, uniformity, and resource bounds are separate claims proved by [[thm-qc-bounded-error-amplification-correct]].

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ be mutually independent Bernoulli$(p_i)$ variables on a finite probability space. Set $S=\sum_iX_i$ and $\mu=\sum_i p_i$. For $\delta\ge0$,
$$\mathbb P(S\ge(1+\delta)\mu)\le\exp\{-\mu((1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta)\}.$$
For $0\le\delta<1$,
$$\mathbb P(S\le(1-\delta)\mu)\le\exp\{-\mu(\delta+(1-\delta)\log(1-\delta))\}.$$
For $0\le\delta\le1$ the upper and lower tails are respectively at most $\exp(-\mu\delta^2/3)$ and $\exp(-\mu\delta^2/2)$, and
$$\mathbb P(|S-\mu|\ge\delta\mu)\le2\exp(-\mu\delta^2/3).$$
At $\delta=1$ the lower optimized bound is $\exp(-\mu)$, proved directly rather than by taking $\log0$. Empty sums and $\mu=0$ are included. Also, for $N>0$ and $t\ge0$,
$$\mathbb P(|S-\mu|\ge t)\le2\exp(-2t^2/N).$$

For every finite promise computation, every length $n$, and every classical input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, the output weights $p_{C_n}(z\mid x)$ from [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] are nonnegative and sum to one over $z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}$. The acceptance probability is the probability of the event $\{z:A_n(x,z)=1\}$, lies in $[0,1]$, and agrees with the finite computational-basis POVM outcome law on the named output register.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

If the generator in [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]] halts on input $1^n$ within $T(n)\le c(n+1)^k$ transitions, then the generated description has length at most $n+T(n)+O(1)$. Consequently its number of gates and total number of wires are polynomial in $n$. This is a full-list size bound; it does not establish equivalence with indexed-gate uniformity.

An **oracle-aware full-list family** has an access specification and a deterministic polynomial-time full-list generator on unary input $1^n$, with the same machine, clock, and final-tape conventions as [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]. The access specification gives, at each length $n$, finitely many named ports $\mathcal O_{n,j}$, each a unitary on a positive number $k_{n,j}$ of qubits. These are mathematical unitary data supplied by the access specification, not matrices computed by the generator. For a parametrized oracle instance, fix that instance throughout a computation and all its repetitions. The generator, printed descriptors, and final classical predicate are independent of the hidden instance: its influence enters only through the granted unitary ports. Any public parameters are fixed explicitly as part of the family specification; oracle comparisons hold them fixed. A port acts only on the wires in its occurrence; there is no persistent private oracle memory, stochastic resampling, or communication between disjoint occurrences through hidden registers.

Each port has a descriptor: a distinct nonempty binary name, its width $k_{n,j}$, and four grant bits for forward, inverse, controlled-forward, and controlled-inverse access. equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

derivations.claim: Fix a promised input $x$. For each input bit $x_i\in\{0,1\}$, the basis action of CNOT maps $|x_i\rangle|0\rangle^{\otimes(r-1)}$ to $|x_i\rangle^{\otimes r}$; applying this independently to each position produces $r$ exact copies of $|x\rangle$. This uses only a computational-basis input and asserts no cloning of arbitrary superpositions. By [F7], CNOT has the required basis action. The $r$ base circuits then act on disjoint full wire blocks, so by [A1] the prepared joint state is $\psi_x^{\otimes r}$, where $\psi_x$ is the single-run output state. For any output strings $z_1,\ldots,z_r$, its joint probability is $$\sum_{w_1,\ldots,w_r}\prod_{i=1}^r|\langle P_O\psi_x,e_{z_i,w_i}\rangle_{\rm root}|^2=\prod_{i=1}^r p_C(z_i\mid x),$$ by finite distributivity and [F4]. Hence the measured output strings are mutually independent with the single-run law, and $X_i=\mathbf1_{\{A_n(x,z_i)=1\}}$ are independent Bernoulli variables with common parameter $p=p_C(x)$.

In ordinary mode [F6] bounds the base description length, operation count, and width polynomially. In oracle mode the same bounds follow directly from the explicit code: a machine started on $n$ input cells and run for $T(n)$ transitions can print at most $n+T(n)+1$ bits, each record occupies at least one bit, and the width is unary. The clocks and bit lengths of $\alpha,\beta,\delta,s$ are polynomial, so $r$ is polynomial. In either mode the repeated circuit uses exactly $r g(C_n)+n(r-1)$ operations and $r w(C_n)$ wires. Copying a record changes each wire index by a block offset with $O(\log(rw(C_n)+2))$ bits; the unary total-wire header has length $r w(C_n)$, and the extra CNOT list has $n(r-1)$ records. In oracle mode each original record's explicit list of wires is copied in full, its port/variant identifier is unchanged, and the entire descriptor table is copied once. Hence the complete repeated description has polynomial length and is produced in polynomial time by running the supplied machines, scanning and copying the base list, and adding offsets by binary arithmetic. These are polynomially many operations on polynomially many bits, implementable by repeated scans on the one-tape machine. A serial layering gives depth at most the total operation count.

Put $S=\sum_{i=1}^rX_i$ and $\mu=rp$. The output predicate accepts exactly when $S\ge r(\alpha+\beta)/2$. If $x$ is YES, then $p\ge\alpha$ and $$\mu-r(\alpha+\beta)/2=r(p-\alpha)+r(\alpha-\beta)/2\ge r/(2s).$$ Thus a false rejection is contained in $\{|S-\mu|\ge r/(2s)\}$.

If $x$ is NO, then $p\le\beta$ and $$r(\alpha+\beta)/2-\mu=r(\alpha-\beta)/2+r(\beta-p)\ge r/(2s).$$ Thus a false acceptance is contained in the same two-sided deviation event $\{|S-\mu|\ge r/(2s)\}$.

In oracle mode no added CNOT record is a query slot, while each original slot occurs exactly once per block. Therefore $g_{\rm ord}(C_n^{\rm rep})=r g_{\rm ord}(C_n)+n(r-1)$ and $N_{j,v}(C_n^{\rm rep})=rN_{j,v}(C_n)$. Summing over variants gives $q_j(C_n^{\rm rep})=rq_j(C_n)$; multiplying each variant count by its unchanged declared charge and summing gives $Q_j(C_n^{\rm rep})=rQ_j(C_n)$. Raw call counts are at most the total operation count; large binary-encoded charges do not justify an unconditional polynomial charged-cost bound. The construction uses no new inverse or controlled access. The same instantiated unitary ports act independently on the disjoint blocks, so the factorization in step 1.1 remains valid, and [F4] applies to each instantiated finite unitary circuit. Ordinary mode contains no oracle slots and remains a circuit over exactly the original library.

Finite event probabilities are sums of nonnegative weights by [F2], so containment makes the probability of either error event in step 2.1 and step 2.2 at most that of the deviation event. Apply [F3] with $t=r/(2s)$; its probability is at most $2\exp(-r/(2s^2))$. Since $\delta=u/v$ with $u\ge1$, $\delta\ge1/v$ and $v\ge2$. Therefore $$\ln(2/\delta)\le\ln(2v)=\ln2+\ln v<1+\ell(v),$$ because $\ln2<1$ and $\ln v=(\ln2)\log_2v<\log_2v<\ell(v)$. Substituting $r=2s^2(\ell(v)+1)$ gives $2\exp(-r/(2s^2))<2\exp(-\ln(2/\delta))=\delta$. This proves both promised error bounds without evaluating an irrational logarithm.

For the declared interfaces covered by the Statement, the input-copy CNOTs act only on the repeated data registers. On the declared ancillary registers the copy unitary is the identity; composing it with the $r$ blockwise exact contracts therefore preserves the clean or dirty return condition, with data target equal to the product of the base targets composed after that copy unitary. Their declared counts are multiplied by $r$; the $n(r-1)$ additional zero-start input-copy wires remain included in total width, with no claim that they return clean. The output predicate runs $A_n$ on each of the $r$ strings, counts successes, computes the rational threshold by exact integer additions and multiplications, and compares the two integers. These operations use polynomial time and space in the polynomially many input bits. Together with step 1.2 and step 2.3, this proves the claimed separate resource bounds and exact query scaling.

A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to **BQP in the QC14 model** when there exist a full-list uniform family $(C_n)$ and a polynomial-time acceptance predicate $A_n$ as in [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]] and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] such that, for every $x\in Y$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\ge\frac23,$$
and for every $x\in N$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\le\frac13.$$
By [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]], $p_{C_n}(x)$ is the probability of the specified acceptance event and lies in $[0,1]$. No condition is imposed for $x\notin Y\cup N$ ([[def-promise-problem]]). The gate alphabet is exactly $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$; its matrix entries lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt2)$ as specified by [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]. This definition does not assert a BQP-versus-classical separation, nor does it assert an unproved equivalence with another circuit-uniformity convention.

Assume the input family, rational threshold functions, gap polynomial, and clocks satisfy the valid-input conditions of [[alg-qc-bounded-error-amplification]]. Assume also that the base acceptance satisfies $p_{C_n}(x)\ge\alpha(n)$ for every length-$n$ YES input and $p_{C_n}(x)\le\beta(n)$ for every length-$n$ NO input, where $0\le\beta(n)<\alpha(n)\le1$ and $\alpha(n)-\beta(n)\ge1/s(n)$. On every input in the YES promise set, the amplified acceptance probability is at least $1-\delta(n)$; on every input in the NO promise set, it is at most $\delta(n)$. If $g(C_n)$ and $w(C_n)$ are the base gate count and total wire count, the repeated family has gate count $r(n)g(C_n)+n(r(n)-1)$ and width $r(n)w(C_n)$. Its depth, complete-description length, generator time, and classical predicate time and space are polynomial in $n$. Ordinary mode retains the exact original fixed gate library and full-list code. In oracle mode its ordinary gate count is $r(n)g_{\rm ord}(C_n)+n(r(n)-1)$, every port/variant count satisfies $N_{j,v}(C_n^{\rm rep})=r(n)N_{j,v}(C_n)$, and both raw query counts $q_j$ and charged query costs $Q_j$ are multiplied by $r(n)$ with the same granted access. Raw query counts are polynomial; charged query costs are polynomial whenever the base charged costs are polynomial. For a base clean or dirty interface whose declared ancillary register is disjoint from the first $n$ input wires, the input-copy stage acts only on data, and the corresponding exact contract is preserved with its declared register count multiplied by $r(n)$; the extra input-copy wires remain in total width and are not counted as returned clean ancillas.

derivations.claim: If the promise problem is in BQP, take $\alpha=2/3$, $\beta=1/3$, and $s=3$. Use the all-length rational target $\widehat\delta(n)=2^{-q(n)}$ when $q(n)\ge2$ and $\widehat\delta(n)=1/4$ otherwise, and apply [F2]. Retain the amplified circuit and predicate where $q(n)\ge2$, and retain the original circuit and predicate at the remaining lengths; this polynomial-time length test preserves full-list uniformity. The rational values have polynomial bit length because $q$ is polynomially bounded, and the gap is $1/3$, so this gives the second family at those lengths. At any length with $q(n)=0$, the target bounds are $p\ge0$ on YES and $p\le1$ on NO; with $q(n)=1$, they are $p\ge1/2$ and $p\le1/2$. The original $2/3,1/3$ bounds imply each of these finite exceptional cases.

A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to **BQP in the QC14 model** when there exist a full-list uniform family $(C_n)$ and a polynomial-time acceptance predicate $A_n$ as in [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]] and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] such that, for every $x\in Y$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\ge\frac23,$$
and for every $x\in N$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\le\frac13.$$
By [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]], $p_{C_n}(x)$ is the probability of the specified acceptance event and lies in $[0,1]$. No condition is imposed for $x\notin Y\cup N$ ([[def-promise-problem]]). The gate alphabet is exactly $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$; its matrix entries lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt2)$ as specified by [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]. This definition does not assert a BQP-versus-classical separation, nor does it assert an unproved equivalence with another circuit-uniformity convention.

A **promise problem** is a pair $(Y,N)$ of disjoint subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$. Its promise is $Y\cup N$. A deterministic solver must accept every word of $Y$ and reject every word of $N$, with either answer allowed elsewhere. The pair belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseP}$ if such a solver has a polynomial time bound on every input.

It belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseNP}$ if there are a polynomial $p$ and a deterministic polynomial-time predicate $V(x,w)$ such that every $x\in Y$ has some $w$ with $|w|\le p(|x|)$ and $V(x,w)=1$, whereas for every $x\in N$ every such $w$ has $V(x,w)=0$. The promise need not be decidable; either side or both sides may be empty. When $Y\cup N=\{0,1\}^*$, this is the ordinary language decision convention.

A **full-list uniform quantum circuit family** is a sequence $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ together with one fixed deterministic one-tape Turing machine $G$ and constants $c\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N$ such that, on input the unary word $1^n$, $G$ halts within $c(n+1)^k$ transitions and its final tape is a valid self-delimiting binary description of the entire circuit $C_n$. The machine output convention is that of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]] and [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and running time is as in [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

The following fixed-order code makes the full circuit and its designated input/output wires effective. A unary natural $r\in\mathbb N$ is written $1^r0$, including the one-symbol code $0$ for $r=0$. A self-delimiting binary natural $r$ is written $1^{|\operatorname{bin}(r)|}0\operatorname{bin}(r)$, where $\operatorname{bin}(r)$ is its ordinary binary numeral with no leading zeros and $\operatorname{bin}(0)=0$. The header gives the input-wire count $n$ and total wire count $m$ in unary, followed by the gate count $g$ as a self-delimiting natural; validity requires $m\ge n$.

Each gate record consists of a two-bit label ($00,01,10,11$ for $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$ respectively), followed by one self-delimiting wire index for $H,T,T^\dagger$ and two ordered self-delimiting indices for CNOT. Every index is less than $m$; CNOT indices are distinct, with the first the control and the second the target. The list contains exactly $g$ records. After the gate list, an output-count self-delimiting natural is followed by that many ordered, pairwise distinct wire indices, each less than $m$. Parsing rejects every other label, malformed or out-of-range index, repeated output index, truncated field, or trailing bit. This defines a total decoder by returning a fixed malformed-code symbol on any invalid word; effective binary encodings and total decoders are as in [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]].

The gate labels and matrices are the fixed finite library $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$ of [[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]], with entries in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt2)$; CNOT is control-first. The remaining $m-n$ wires are auxiliary wires; their initial states are determined when a family is used in a computation model. This family convention adopts full-list generation. It makes no equivalence claim with indexed-gate uniformity and, in particular, does not assert that an indexed-gate generator can be expanded to the full list in polynomial time.

derivations.claim: The pair is a promise problem because $Y$ and $N$ are disjoint singletons of distinct one-bit words, as required by [F2]. For $n\ge1$, use input count $n$, total wire count $m=n$, gate count zero, and output tuple $(0)$. For $n=0$, use input count zero, total wire count one, gate count zero, and output tuple $(0)$, whose wire is initialized to zero. These are valid descriptions under [F3]. One fixed one-tape generator writes the two unary counts by repeated sweeps over the $n$ input marks and then appends the constant gate-count and output fields; at most $O((n+1)^2)$ transitions suffice. The total predicate is $1$ exactly when $x$ is the one-bit word $0$ and $z=0$, and $0$ otherwise, so it is deterministic and polynomial time.

On the YES input $x=0$, the identity circuit leaves the measured output in $|0\rangle$, so acceptance is $1\ge2/3$. On the NO input $x=1$, it leaves the measured output in $|1\rangle$, so acceptance is $0\le1/3$. Every other string is outside $Y\cup N$, where [F1] imposes no condition. Hence this promise problem is in BQP in the stated model.
